name: Bilal Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I'm not much of a talker about this stuff, but if it's private I'll be straight with you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the wooden and plywood moulds that concrete gets poured into, mostly floors and walls on blocks of flats. I'm on site at Canal Road by half seven, we strip yesterday's panels, clean them, oil them and set them up again for the next pour. I like the pour days, everyone's switched on and it's like a team sport. What wears me out is the cold and the waiting, because if the concrete lorry's late we just stand there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure does the work feel right now, before we get to any pictures?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not very, if I'm honest. Hartley Frames, the firm I work for, is a subcontractor, so when the main contractor stops paying on time we get laid off for a week with no notice. I've got maybe two weeks of rent saved, and my girlfriend Tamsin works nights in a care home, so we're both on low money. There's maybe two other formwork firms within an hour of here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly that sounds like now. The office got some new software for timesheets and that's about it for AI round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. The lads on site have been saying for ages it's all talk for people in offices. I'd probably still say we need a proper union deal on site, because the problems we've got were never about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm still stuck with the same mess. Nothing radical changes, which means the layoffs between jobs carry on, rent keeps going up, and Hartley keeps paying the lowest rate in the area. AI being hype doesn't fix any of that for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now really, keep turning up and keep my head down. I'd cut the takeaway on Fridays and try to put fifty a week away so I've got more than two weeks' rent. And I'd push the lads to sign up with the union branch, because there's only three of us in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not scary like the other stuff might be, it's just the same grind with no way up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the layoffs between jobs carry on. What happens in a week like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March we had nine days off with no pay. I borrowed from my brother Kieran to cover the rent and I still owe him some of it. The main contractor had a dispute, and Tamsin picked up two extra night shifts, which wrecked her for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for those weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The developers and the big contractors who squeeze the subbies, and the government for letting them. Hartley isn't evil, they just get squeezed and pass it down to us. Nobody at the top ever goes without pay for nine days.

say: **AI hype** was always office talk, and the lads on site said so all along.
Site workers still need a **union deal**, because our problems were never about computers.
think: Nothing radical changing means the **layoffs** between jobs and rising **rent** carry on.
AI flopping does nothing to lift **Hartley's** low pay rate.
do: Cut the **Friday takeaway** and put about **fifty** a week aside.
Recruit site workmates into the **union branch**, which has only three members.
Keep turning up at **Canal Road** and keep his head down.
feel: Worn down by the **same grind**, rather than scared.
S0.quote: Last March we had nine days off with no pay. I borrowed from my brother Kieran to cover the rent and I still owe him some of it.
fieldNote: Already **anxious** before AI enters: unpaid layoff weeks, two weeks' rent saved, few other firms nearby.
Blames **developers and contractors** squeezing subcontractors, not his own employer.
Resistant to change but sees **collective action** as the one lever he has.

steps.text: Drop the Friday takeaway and save about fifty a week toward rent
Sign up at least two more Hartley workmates to the union branch
Keep working formwork at the Canal Road flats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so this one is more for the people in offices first. Robots come into our stuff slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who should worry first, the estimators and the people booking deliveries. On site I'd tell people our job is safe for a good while, because nobody's building a robot that can strip formwork in the rain. I'd probably post something about protecting jobs, since that's what I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't know. If the planning and ordering goes to software, Hartley might need fewer site managers, and then those blokes come down and take jobs like mine. And I've never used any of these AI tools, so if the job starts needing them I'm behind already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and see what happens at Hartley, because there's nothing else nearby anyway. I'd ask the union branch to get something in writing about new tech, like no one gets laid off without training first. And I'd keep putting a bit away, maybe up it to seventy a week if overtime allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit sick in the stomach. It's like the ground's moving slowly and I can't tell which way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used AI tools. If Hartley asked you to use one on a tablet tomorrow, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get one of the younger lads to show me, then try to get out of it. I can read a drawing fine on paper. I don't trust a screen telling me where a wall goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tamsin's work in the care home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her work is people, washing and lifting and talking to the old folks, so I don't think software touches that much. Maybe the rotas and the paperwork. If anything, she's safer than me, which is funny because she earns less.

say: Office jobs like **estimators** and delivery booking should worry first, not site carpenters.
Nobody is building a robot that can **strip formwork** in the rain.
think: Displaced **site managers** might drop down and compete for jobs like his.
Never using **AI tools** leaves him behind if the job starts to need them.
do: Stay at **Hartley** and watch, since no other firms are nearby.
Ask the union branch for a **written promise** of training before any layoffs.
Raise savings to about **seventy a week** when overtime allows.
feel: Uneasy and **sick in the stomach**, unsure which way things will move.
S1.quote: I can read a drawing fine on paper. I don't trust a screen telling me where a wall goes.
fieldNote: Correctly sees **thinking tasks** go first, but fears managers being pushed down onto site jobs.
His **avoidance** of tech shows: he'd get a younger worker to cover for him.
Thinks his girlfriend's **care work** is safer than his own job.

steps.text: Stay at Hartley and watch whether site manager jobs get cut
Ask the union branch to win written training-before-layoff terms
Raise savings to seventy a week from overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's nothing. And then robots three years after that, so 2031 for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in right now, before it's too late. Tax the companies that use the robots and pay people properly while they retrain. I'd be at any protest going, and I'd say that out loud on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm done in the trade by about 2031. The first two years, the office stuff goes and Hartley keeps us on, maybe even busy. But after that a robot that can do formwork as well as me doesn't need a lunch break or a sick day. I'd be 32 with no savings and nothing else I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every bit of the union campaign, because that's the only thing I trust. I'd cut everything I can, no car, get the bus, so we're not drowning when it hits. And I'd talk to Tamsin about whether care work could take me, because people looking after people might be the last thing left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, and angry that nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 2028 for the office side and 2031 for the robots. What would those three years in between be like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the weirdest years of my life, working flat out while knowing the clock's ticking. Builders would want everything poured before the robots come and drop the price. I'd take every hour going and try to save, but with what Hartley pays that's still not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tamsin the night you heard about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm sorry, I don't have a plan B. She'd say we'll figure it out, she always does. But I'd lie awake doing sums.

say: The **government** must step in now and tax firms that use robots.
Workers deserve **proper pay** while they retrain, and he'd join any protest.
think: Expects to be **out of the trade** by about 2031, aged 32.
Has **no savings** and no other skill to fall back on.
do: Join every part of the **union campaign** on automation.
Sell the **car** and take the bus to cut costs.
Ask Tamsin about moving into **care work**, which may last longest.
feel: Properly **scared**, and **angry** that workers were never asked.
S2.quote: A robot that can do formwork as well as me doesn't need a lunch break or a sick day.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** between AGI and robots feels to him like a countdown, not a reprieve.
Thin savings and few local jobs make this **alarmed**, not just anxious.
Turns to **care work** through his girlfriend, the first career idea he has raised.

steps.text: Join the union's campaign on robots on building sites
Sell the car and take the bus to work
Ask Tamsin's care home about trainee care worker jobs
Vote and protest for a tax on firms that replace workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the AI, eight years for the robots. That's 2034. I'd be 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, we need protection, but I'd say it with a bit less panic. I'd say there's time to get the unions and the government ready if they actually bother. Online I'd share stuff about retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same end, just later. I'm not great with change, so having a few years mostly means I'd keep putting it off. That worries me more than the date does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe get the overtime up. I'd get my scaffolding ticket, because that's still hands-on and people would want it till the last minute. And I'd keep pushing the union branch to talk about this now, not in 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slower worry. Like a bill I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep putting it off. What would make you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone I know lose their job to it. My mate Darren drives a crane and if they automate his crane, I'll know it's real. Until then I'd probably tell myself it's still talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the scaffolding ticket really help if robots arrive in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever, you're right. It just buys me a couple more years of the work I know. I'm not going to suddenly become a programmer.

say: Workers need **protection**, and there is time to prepare if anyone bothers.
think: Same **end point**, just later, so he expects it still reaches him.
Fears his own habit of **putting things off** more than the date.
do: Keep working and push **overtime** to build savings in the first year.
Get a **scaffolding ticket** to stay in hands-on work longer.
Push the **union branch** to plan for robots now.
feel: A slower **worry**, like a bill he knows is coming.
S3.quote: I'm not great with change, so having a few years mostly means I'd keep putting it off.
fieldNote: Admits that **extra time** won't help a person who avoids change, which is unusually honest.
His trigger to act is a **friend's job** going, not news.
Still expects to lose his trade, so mood stays **alarmed** despite the slower pace.

steps.text: Work every overtime shift and save it toward a rent cushion
Get a scaffolding ticket to stay in hands-on site work
Push the union branch to bargain over site robots now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 for the brain side, 2039 for robots. I'd be pushing 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this properly, if we start now. Proper retraining for site workers, paid for by the people making the money. I'd say that at the pub and on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the only one where I think I can come out okay. I'd have time to learn a different thing slowly, the way I learn, and maybe Tamsin and I could save a bit. But I know me, and I'd waste the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a night course in something like building maintenance or care, something with people in it. I'd keep at Hartley for now because there's nothing else. And I'd try to get Tamsin and me into a council flat so the rent stops going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less scared. Still nervous, but it feels like there's a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where people still want a person, like fixing things in people's homes or working in care with Tamsin. I don't need a big job. I just want to not be scared of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first few years. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union ran a course on site, I'd go. If it's me on my own on a computer at night, I won't. Everyone doing it together makes it normal, that's just the truth.

say: A **decade** is enough to prepare site workers properly if the work starts now.
Firms making the money should **pay for retraining**.
think: This is the only picture where he thinks he can **come out okay**.
Expects to **waste the first years** unless training is part of normal site life.
do: Look into a **night course** in building maintenance or care work.
Stay at **Hartley** for now, since there is nothing else nearby.
Apply for a **council flat** with Tamsin to stop rent rises.
feel: Less **scared**, still nervous, but sees **a door**.
S4.quote: If the union ran a course on site, I'd go. If it's me on my own on a computer at night, I won't.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into **cautious hope**, but thin savings and few local jobs keep him **anxious**.
Learns best in a **group on site**, not alone online.
Wants a modest life: work with people and **steady rent**.

steps.text: Sign up for a night course in building maintenance
Keep formwork job at Hartley while studying
Apply with Tamsin for a council flat with fixed rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. What would help is real money while you retrain, not a website, and the union having a say in how fast robots come onto sites. And cheaper rent, honestly, because that's what makes everything else scary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't on the books. Half the lads on some sites are cash-in-hand, and when robots come they won't even show up in the numbers. Nobody will count them losing their jobs.

headlineQuote: Half the lads on some sites are cash-in-hand, and when robots come they won't even show up in the numbers. Nobody will count them losing their jobs.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old formwork carpenter** working for a subcontractor on a block of flats.
He has about **two weeks' rent** saved and has already borrowed from his brother during an unpaid layoff.
He lives with Tamsin, a **night-shift care worker**, and they are both on low pay.
He trusts the **union** and blames developers and government, but avoids any new technology himself.
His fear rises with speed, from **anxious** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 would end his trade with no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining money**, a union say on site robots, and **cheaper rent**.
